detail.longDescription:
Honestly, Tuta Mail’s aggressive marketing coming out of every corner of the internet is getting exhausting. Everywhere you look, it’s the same fairy tales about "the world's most secure email," "quantum-safe encryption," and absolute privacy for your correspondence.

If you actually buy into the hype and decide to sign up for an account, keep a few things in mind upfront—things those glossy ad banners conveniently leave out:

* **No OpenPGP and zero interoperability.** Tuta lives inside its own proprietary walled garden. End-to-end encryption works by default only between Tuta users. If the person you're emailing uses a regular provider or standard PGP, tough luck: your message either goes out in plaintext, or you have to send them a password-protected link so they can read it through Tuta’s web interface. Importing your existing PGP keys—or exporting them when you decide to leave—is impossible.
* **Forget about IMAP, POP3, and SMTP.** You can't hook your inbox up to Thunderbird, K-9 Mail, or mutt, nor can you set up proper local backups using standard tools. Want to read your email? You're forced to use their proprietary app or a web browser.
* **German jurisdiction and everything that comes with it.** The service is based in Germany, and under a German court order, the company is legally required to enable real-time monitoring on a targeted account and hand over all unencrypted incoming and outgoing emails to law enforcement (which means pretty much all standard external correspondence). On top of that, metadata—who emailed whom and when—isn't encrypted at all.
* **Free accounts vanish after six months.** If you create a backup inbox or one for occasional sign-ups and don't log in for more than 6 months, it gets wiped for inactivity along with everything inside it.
* **Anonymity on your dime—and through hoops.** There's no direct crypto checkout when subscribing—only credit cards, PayPal, or app stores. If you want to pay with Bitcoin, Monero, or cash, you have to go through a third-party reseller (Proxystore) to buy gift vouchers. Meanwhile, trying to register a free account over Tor or a popular VPN frequently ends in an IP block.

At the end of the day, instead of freedom and control over your own keys, you get a closed ecosystem wrapped in strict German *Ordnung*. Standard PGP on top of a normal mail provider—or self-hosting your own mail server—at least doesn't pretend to protect you from the very authorities it's legally obligated to let through the front door on the first court order.
